You use the Present Perfect tense in variety of ways.

In a story, you can use it to:

  • refer to events that happened very recently. In these cases, you use words like just, only just and recently.

    For example:
    Entering Tibet you feel as though you've just entered an entirely different world.
You can use the Present Perfect in questions to ask about past experience or unusual events:

• notice the use of the word ever in questions.

You can use words such as yet, up to now, so far and until now when you use the Present Perfect, since these words and phrases refer to a period of time covering the past to the present.

For example:
Up to now, these areas have not required permits to visit.
The traditional Tibetan culture has remained strong until now and is central to the region.
Here, the original Tibetan culture has survived unchanged so far.
If you haven't yet, don't.

Skimming and scanning are two very different strategies for reading texts quickly and for getting the information you need from them without wasting time.
Knowing when to use these skills will help with your reading abilities and comprehension skills.

Skimming:

Skimming refers to looking only for the general or main ideas in a text.

When you skim, your overall understanding is reduced because you don't read everything. You read only what is important to your purpose.

One technique for effective skimming is reading only the first line of each paragraph, since these are the topic sentences which will give you some clues about what the main idea of each paragraph is.

Scanning:

Scanning refers to looking for specific information in a text. Examples of scanning in daily life are: bus schedules, movie schedules, phone lists, etc. When you use these kinds of texts, you are only looking for a specific detail (a number, a date, a name, etc.).

Knowing the structure of the text you want to scan will help you do it quickly (alphabetical, numerical, categorical, chronological).
Try skimming and scanning the text for the general ideas and for specifics.

images.text:
Entering Tibet, you feel as though you've just entered an entirely different world. The traditional Tibetan culture has remained strong until now and is central to the region.
Northern Tibet, or Amdo is home to the nomadic people. Huge grasslands typify the area. It also maintains a rich culture. To the north, you can find numerous interesting monasteries. Eastern Tibet, or Kham is mountainous with deep valleys where swift rivers run through.

Both areas are wonderful to explore. Here, the original Tibetan culture has survived unchanged so far, unlike the culture in the big cities of modern Tibet. Up to now, these areas have not required permits to visit.
Tourism in Tibet is now strictly controlled by the Chinese government. This means that tourists have recently had to start traveling with organized trips. They haven't been allowed to travel on an independent basis. Have you thought of trying to go off on your own? If you haven't yet, don't. There are checkpoints everywhere. You may even be stopped or questioned by the Chinese police.

Eating in Tibet can be monotonous. The diet is largely limited to barley with mutton or yak and dairy products. There are few spices or vegetables, except for a brutally hot chili sauce often served on the side. Stop in a Chinese restaurant for an excellent wider variety of food.
The Tibet experience is still worth dealing with the permits and restrictions. I've only just returned and would not have missed any of it for the world!
